query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of interstitial carbon into a refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a baseline NbMoTaW alloy) will synergistically improve both yield strength and ductility by promoting the formation of finely dispersed carbide precipitates that serve as dual obstacles to dislocation motion and as local modifiers of the deformation mechanism (e.g., by facilitating twinning or transformation‐induced plasticity).
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory HEA based on refractory elements (e.g., NbMoTaW) with a nearly single‐phase, largely BCC matrix lacking significant secondary phases or nano‐precipitates.
generation.intervention: Alloy the baseline refractory HEA with a low interstitial content (on the order of 0.5–1 at.% carbon) during melting, followed by a homogenization annealing treatment to uniformly distribute carbon and promote controlled nano‐scale carbide precipitation.
generation.conditions: Samples are processed via arc melting and homogenized, then cold‐rolled and annealed to achieve a fine microstructure. Room temperature tensile tests under quasi-static loading (strain rate ~10^–3 s^–1) will be used to evaluate mechanical properties.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniformly dispersed nano‐sized carbide precipitates and refined grain boundaries that result from carbon interstitial alloying.
generation.mechanism: The fine carbide precipitates act to hinder dislocation motion (improving strength) while also locally modifying stacking fault energies to facilitate additional plastic deformation mechanisms (e.g., nano‐twinning or TRIP), thereby promoting a simultaneous increase in ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the carbon‐free baseline, the carbon-alloyed refractory HEA is expected to exhibit a higher yield strength and a greater uniform elongation, thus reducing the typical strength–ductility trade-off.
generation.baseline: Refractory high-entropy alloy such as NbMoTaW fabricated without interstitial carbon addition.
generation.boundary: The improvement is anticipated under room-temperature deformation conditions with controlled carbon additions; if the carbon level is too high or if processing conditions lead to coarse carbides, the beneficial effect may be lost and embrittlement may occur.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal carbon content and stability of the nano-carbide precipitates under long-term service or varied temperature conditions are still subject to further exploration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples based on NbMoTaW: one as a control (no carbon) and one with an optimized interstitial carbon level (e.g., ~0.7 at.%). Ensure both sets undergo identical melting, homogenization, and thermomechanical processing. Characterize the microstructure (using TEM and XRD) to confirm the presence and distribution of nano-carbide precipitates in the carbon-alloyed samples. Then, conduct room-temperature quasi-static tensile tests and in-situ microstructural observations during deformation.
measurements: Nano-precipitate size and distribution from TEM
Evidence of twinning or phase transformation (TRIP/TWIP) via in-situ imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-alloyed samples do not display a statistically significant simultaneous enhancement in yield strength and ductility relative to the carbon-free baseline, or if the microstructural analysis shows no formation of beneficial nano-carbide precipitates (or shows formation of coarse, brittle carbides), the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Exploring strong and yet ductile materials is paramount for reducing the weight and hence the energy consumption in all fields where mobile structures are used,. However, strength and ductility of current engineering materials are generally conflicting, limiting traditional alloy design strategies. Over the past years, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have drawn great attention as it opens an entirely new realm of compositional opportunities for designing novel materials with exceptional properties,,,,,,,. HEAs were originally proposed to contain multiple principal elements in near-equimolar ratios to stabilize single-phase solid solutions through maximizing configurational entropy,. Recently, motivated by the fact that maximized configurational entropy is not the sole factor determining phase stability of HEAs,,,,, a novel metastable transformation-induced plasticity dual-phase (TRIP-DP) HEA with exceptional strength and ductility has been developed,. Based on this approach, we propose a new class of HEAs which is interstitially alloyed and unifies all known metallic strengthening mechanisms in one material.
